implementation.name: original-v1-kv-cache-growth
implementation.scope: Canonical 70B-class GQA model, FP16 KV, INT4 weights and the original H100 budget. A uniform-context batch is used for clarity. Capacity excludes runtime workspace, as in the source. Markers use the original curves and axes; motion is illustrative, not latency.
implementation.question: How do active requests compete with context length?

purpose: Why does one new token retain more memory?

storyboard.label: Admit 32 requests at 4,096 tokens
storyboard.description: All 32 requests retain their own history. Resident weights have already been subtracted from the capacity shown.

storyboard.label: Extend every request to 4,800 tokens
storyboard.description: Appending records preserves all earlier token records. The same batch now approaches the post-weight cache budget.

storyboard.label: Try extending to 5,000 tokens
storyboard.description: The requested cache would exceed the budget. Admission is rejected here; the actual retained cache stays at 4,800 tokens. Real engines must reject, queue, evict, or change scheduling before exceeding capacity.

storyboard.label: Finish and release half the requests
storyboard.description: Sixteen completed requests release their private cache records after their last readers finish. The remaining sixteen retain their 4,800-token histories.

storyboard.label: Extend remaining requests to 8,192 tokens
storyboard.description: With fewer simultaneous histories, longer contexts fit. Earlier records remain in each surviving request cache.

storyboard.label: Finish and release eight more requests
storyboard.description: Release reduces the resident cache without changing context length for the surviving eight requests.

storyboard.label: Extend the eight survivors to 16,000 tokens
storyboard.description: The same linear relationship applies between the plotted batch-size curves. No token eviction or recomputation is modeled.

guard: Exact canonical model budget. Rejecting a target never commits over-budget records. Markers and capacity bar show same retained state; no runtime workspace, token eviction, or timing model.
